subject: Science
theme: pathophysiology of diabetes mellitus - hyperglycemia and insulin regulation
question_short_text: Which associations characterize diabetes mellitus: higher/lower blood sugar and insulin levels?
text:
Which of the following are associated with diabetes mellitus, a common disease in adults?

I. Higher sugar level in blood
II. Lower sugar level in blood
III. Lower insulin level in blood
IV. Higher insulin level in blood
explanation: Diabetes mellitus is characterized by hyperglycemia (higher blood glucose) resulting from deficient or ineffective insulin. In type 1 diabetes, the pancreas cannot produce adequate insulin (lower insulin level). In type 2 diabetes, insulin production may be impaired or cells resist insulin action, both leading to lower effective insulin levels and accumulation of glucose in the blood.

research.summary: The core of this question is the fundamental mechanism of diabetes mellitus: the relationship between insulin insufficiency and blood glucose accumulation. Diabetes is uniformly characterized by hyperglycemia—sustained elevated blood glucose—which results from either absolute insulin deficiency (type 1) or relative insulin deficiency combined with insulin resistance (type 2). The trap here is assuming that diabetes involves only high insulin or only low glucose. The defining pathophysiology is that lower or ineffective insulin levels → glucose cannot be transported into cells → glucose accumulates in blood (hyperglycemia). Type 1 diabetics have immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells, producing little to no insulin. Type 2 diabetics have impaired beta-cell function and tissue insulin resistance, meaning circulating insulin levels are insufficient to overcome resistance or normalize glucose uptake. In both cases, the combination is always higher blood sugar and lower (or ineffective) insulin. Statement II (lower blood sugar) is categorically false—diabetes is defined by sustained elevated blood glucose, not low glucose. Statement IV (higher insulin) is also false; insulin levels are either reduced (type 1) or inadequately elevated for the degree of insulin resistance (type 2). The central recognition pattern: if glucose is not being removed from blood efficiently, it will accumulate (high), and the hormone responsible for that removal (insulin) must be deficient or non-functional (low).
facts: Type 1 diabetes accounts for 5–10% of all diabetes cases and involves autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells, resulting in absolute insulin deficiency.

Type 2 diabetes accounts for over 90% of all diabetes cases and involves a combination of impaired insulin secretion and insulin resistance in peripheral tissues, but both lead to insufficient insulin action.

sources.title: Diabetes - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
sources.whyUsed: Confirmed that type 1 results from defective insulin secretion and type 2 from defective insulin secretion and/or action, both leading to hyperglycemia.

sources.whyUsed: Established that deficiency of insulin or insensitivity of its receptors play a central role in all forms of diabetes mellitus, and that insulin normally regulates glucose uptake into cells.
